description: BEESRA brings together innovators passionate about space, engineering, science, and technology. We aim to turn ideas and NASA data into creative solutions through research, programming, data analysis, design, and teamwork. We welcome motivated people from diverse backgrounds who want to learn, share knowledge, build skills, and solve challenging problems. Programmers, engineers, researchers, designers, and creative thinkers are welcome to contribute and grow with us as we explore beyond Earth
summary:
BEESRA Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a Python-based prototype that explores potential lunar landing locations near the Moon's south pole. Using NASA/JPL Horizons data, the project calculates and visualizes the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar horizon at selected locations and times.

The prototype compares two illustrative lunar locations to investigate how sunlight exposure and geometric Earth visibility change over time. These visualizations provide preliminary insights into potential solar-energy opportunities and direct-to-Earth communication visibility.

Our goal is to make astronomical information easier to understand through accessible, data-driven visualization. The project demonstrates how space science, programming, and engineering can contribute to future lunar exploration. It is an early-stage research prototype and does not yet account for detailed local terrain, landing hazards, or complete communication-system performance.
details:
BEESRA Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a Python-based prototype developed using Google Colab and NASA/JPL Horizons API data.

The project retrieves astronomical position data for the Sun and Earth as observed from selected lunar locations. It processes azimuth and elevation angles relative to the lunar horizon and presents the results through graphical visualizations.

The prototype compares two illustrative lunar south-polar locations:

- Site A: 0° longitude, 85° South latitude.
- Site B: 30° East longitude, 85° South latitude.

These comparisons help users explore sunlight exposure and geometric Earth visibility over time, providing preliminary insights into potential solar-energy and communication opportunities.

The project uses Python, NASA/JPL Horizons data, and data visualization to make complex astronomical information easier to understand.

Our goal is to support lunar exploration research and education. Future improvements could include terrain analysis, additional landing locations, and more detailed engineering models.

This is an early-stage research prototype, not a certified lunar landing-site selection or mission-safety system. It does not yet account for detailed local terrain, actual solar-power production, or guaranteed communication availability.
